extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for forming, verifying, and explaining laws of nature—how to judge when a deductive theory or statement of causal law is adequate, more general, or properly explained by other laws. Focuses on the roles of induction, ratiocination, verification, and three modes of resolving laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method consists of three constituent parts: Induction, Ratiocination, and Verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three are essential; without Verification the results of deduction have little other value than conjecture. Deduction alone (without prior induction and subsequent verification) is insufficient to establish reliable laws of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of deductive conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: To warrant reliance on conclusions arrived at by deduction, these conclusions must be found, on careful comparison, to accord with the results of direct observation wherever it can be had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If deductions predict an effect that does not follow in known cases, one must show (or make a probable surmise) what frustrated it; verification is incomplete unless some verifying cases are of at least equal complexity with the cases to which the theory will be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory should deductively lead to empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effectual verification of a theory is that it leads deductively to the empirical laws of the phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a theory accounts for observed uniformities (complete or incomplete), it provides strong evidence—illustrated by Newtonian theory leading to Kepler's laws. The fit between deductive consequences and empirical regularities is a key test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain empirical laws for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws of phenomena should be ascertained, by comparison of instances conformably to the Method of Agreement, to facilitate verification of theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phenomena ought to be described comprehensively and accurately; collecting observations and expressing simplest correct expressions (e.g., planetary places as circle, epicycles, ellipse) aids verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of complex instances as verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex instances which were of no use in discovering a law can still serve as evidence to verify that law once it is obtained otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complex case that conforms to a theory becomes a new experiment on the law, sometimes eliminating previously overlooked circumstances (example: discrepancy in sound velocity explained by heat from condensation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of explanation (law of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A law or uniformity is said to be explained when another law or laws are pointed out, of which that law itself is but a case and from which it could be deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explaining a law consists in resolving it into more general laws and relevant collocations (the existence/combination of agents in circumstances of place and time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode 1 — Resolution into separate laws of causes (composition of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex effect's law is explained by resolving it into the separate laws of the causes which contribute to it, together with the fact of their co-existence (collocations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the laws of the separate causes and proof of their co-existence are required. Example: planetary motion resolved into rectilineal tendency and centripetal force, plus their collocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode 2 — Resolution via intermediate links (proximate vs remote cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: When further observation detects an intermediate link B between apparent cause A and effect C, the sequence A→C is resolved into A→B and B→C; the originally assigned cause may be only a remote cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding intermediate phenomena (e.g., nerve-affection between touch and sensation; chemical intermediate in acid corrosion) makes the explanatory laws more general and shows where exceptions to A→C are likely to be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode 3 — Subsumption under a more general law
rubrics_metrics.description: Several laws (or the same law in different classes of cases) are gathered up under one more general law which includes them all—subsumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsumption requires showing that cases are not merely similar in quality but conform in quantity as well (example: subsuming terrestrial gravity and celestial tendencies under universal gravitation). General laws often arise by combining partial laws observed by different people/times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality and certainty increase under resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law is resolved into other laws (by any of the three modes), the resolving laws are always laws more general than the original; in the first two modes they are also more certain (more universally true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elementary laws are less likely to require limitation by subsequent experience; complex laws (results of combinations) are more liable to be found conditional or fallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex laws are more fragile / liable to failure
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of a complex effect (joint action of causes) is liable to be oftener unfulfilled than any one of the simpler laws of which it is composed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every contingency that defeats any constituent law can defeat the complex law (examples: rust disabling machinery; small changes in force proportions changing orbital conic sections). Prefer explanations in terms of simpler component laws where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsumption requires elimination of circumstantial contingencies
rubrics_metrics.description: To subsume phenomena under a more general law, one must eliminate special circumstances (e.g., proximity to earth) by obtaining observations in different classes of cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining partial observations from different contexts can show that what was thought peculiar is actually common; this elimination process is how broader laws (e.g., gravitation) are established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation extends deductive science but substitutes mysteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation (resolving one law into more general laws) extends the reach of deductive science, but philosophically only substitutes one mystery for another—the more general laws remain 'why'-questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists should understand 'explanation' as pointing to more general laws and collocations from which the partial law follows; avoid treating the general law as a causal producer of the particular merely because it accounts for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical demand: show what frustrated predicted effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When a deductive prediction fails in observed instances, the theory is imperfect unless we can show (or make a probable surmise of) what frustrated the prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification requires accounting for counterexamples by identifying intervening causes, negative conditions, or other collocations that prevent the expected effect; absence of such account undermines reliance on the theory.
